title: Battery chemistries: voltages, charging and dangers
summary: How to tell battery types apart, their safe voltage ranges, how to charge and store each one, and what makes each dangerous. Covers lead-acid, lithium-ion, lithium iron phosphate, nickel, alkaline and lithium primary cells.

steps.text: Read the label: words, size code and voltage. Use the label codes table to name the chemistry.
Measure the resting voltage (no charge or load for a few hours). Compare it with the table. A voltage that doesn't fit the label means a wrong guess or a damaged battery.
Look up its charge voltage and use only a charger made for that chemistry and cell count.
Never mix chemistries, capacities, ages or charge levels in one series string or pack.
Store each type the way the table says, somewhere cool and dry, with terminals covered.

notes:
## The main types

| Chemistry | How to recognise | Nominal per cell | Full, resting | Empty: stop here | Store at | Main dangers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lead-acid (flooded, AGM, gel) | Heavy box, 2, 6 or 12 V; "lead", "VRLA", "AGM", "deep cycle" | 2.0 V (12 V = 6 cells) | 12.7 V or more for a 12 V battery (AGM and gel about 12.8 V) | Trojan's limit is 80% used: about 11.7 V resting for flooded, 11.9 V for AGM, 12.0 V for gel (Trojan guide) | Fully charged; check every 4–6 weeks (flooded) or 2–3 months (AGM, gel) and recharge at 70–75% (Trojan guide) | Sulphuric acid, explosive hydrogen when charging, huge short-circuit current, lead |
| Lithium-ion (cobalt, NMC, NCA) | 18650 and 21700 cylinders, flat pouches; "Li-ion", "ICR", "INR", "NCR", 3.6 or 3.7 V | 3.6–3.7 V | 4.2 V (4.35 V on some "high voltage" cells) | 3.0 V (2.5 V absolute) | 3.6–3.8 V | Fire if punctured, crushed, overcharged, shorted, or charged below 0 °C |
| Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, LFP) | "LiFePO4", "LFP", "IFR", 3.2 V cells, 12.8 V drop-in batteries | 3.2 V (12.8 V = 4 cells) | about 3.35–3.4 V (13.4–13.6 V pack) | 2.5–2.8 V (10–11 V pack); Battle Born's BMS cuts off at 10 V (Battle Born BB10012) | charged and disconnected from all loads; Battle Born recommends storing them full (Battle Born BB10012) | Safest lithium type, but shorts still arc and burn; don't charge below 0 °C, and some packs not below +5 °C: Victron's only from +5 to +50 °C (Victron lithium) |
| Nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) | AA, AAA, C, D, 9 V and packs; "Ni-MH", 1.2 V | 1.2 V | 1.3–1.4 V | 1.0 V | Charged, cool and disconnected; they typically keep 50–80% of their charge after a year (Energizer NiMH) | Gets hot if charged wrongly; small alkaline leaks |
| Nickel-cadmium (NiCd) | Older tools, garden lights, emergency lights; "Ni-Cd", 1.2 V | 1.2 V | 1.3–1.4 V | 1.0 V | Any state | Cadmium is toxic: don't crush or burn |
| Alkaline (not rechargeable) | "Alkaline", "LR6" (AA), "LR03" (AAA), 1.5 V | 1.5 V | 1.5–1.6 V | 0.9–1.0 V | Room temperature | Leaks corrosive crust; can burst if charged |
| Lithium primary (not rechargeable) | "CR" codes (CR2032, CR123A) at 3 V; lithium AA at 1.5 V; sealed alarm and meter cells at 3–3.6 V | 1.5, 3.0 or 3.6 V | as labelled | about 2.0 V for 3 V types | Room temperature; lasts 10 years or more | Fire or burst if charged or shorted |
| Silver oxide and zinc-air buttons | "SR" codes (watches); hearing-aid cells with a peel tab | 1.55 V / 1.4 V | as labelled | about 1.2 V | Sealed in packet | Swallowed button cells burn through the gut within hours: keep from children |

## Charging

| Chemistry | Method | Charge voltage | After full | Gentle charge current |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flooded lead-acid, 12 V | Bulk at constant current, then hold voltage (absorb), then float | 14.4–14.8 V | Float 13.2–13.5 V | 10–13% of the Ah rating (10–13 A for 100 Ah) (Trojan guide) |
| AGM, 12 V | Same | 14.4–14.7 V | Float 13.5–13.8 V | up to 20% of Ah (Trojan guide) |
| Gel, 12 V | Same | 14.1–14.4 V | Float 13.5–13.8 V | 10–13% of Ah (Trojan guide) |
| Lithium-ion, per cell | Constant current, then hold voltage, then stop. No float | 4.20 V, ±50 mV (BU-409) | Stop when current falls to about 3–5% of the Ah rating (BU-409) | Half the capacity in amps (0.5C) or less |
| LiFePO4, per cell | Constant current, then hold voltage, then stop or low float | 3.55–3.65 V (14.2–14.6 V for a 12.8 V pack; Battle Born BB10012, Victron lithium) | Float 3.35–3.4 V (13.4–13.6 V) or none | 0.5C or less (Battle Born BB10012) |
| NiMH and NiCd, per cell | Constant current with a timer or end detection | rises to about 1.45–1.5 V while charging | Trickle below 0.025C (C/40) | 0.1C for 12–14 hours on a simple timer charger (Energizer NiMH) |

Lead-acid charge voltages come down a little in hot weather and up a little in the cold, about 0.03 V per °C for a 12 V battery; good chargers do this with a temperature sensor (Trojan guide). Equalise only flooded batteries, never AGM or gel (Trojan guide), and never use a lead-acid "desulphation" or "equalise" mode on lithium.

## Lead-acid state of charge (12 V, resting, about 25 °C)

| Charge | Flooded | AGM | Gel |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full | 12.7 | 12.8 | 12.8 |
| About 75% | 12.4 | 12.5 | 12.7 |
| About 50% | 12.1 | 12.2 | 12.4 |
| About 25% | 11.7 | 11.9 | 12.0 |
| Nearly flat | 11.5 | 11.6 | 11.8 |

Volts at rest from Trojan's deep-cycle tables (Trojan guide); use your own maker's table if you have it. Nearly flat is 10% charge for flooded (Trojan's flooded table stops there) and 0% for AGM and gel. Rest means no charging or load for at least 6 hours, better 24 (Trojan guide). A lead-acid battery left flat for weeks sulphates and loses capacity for good.

Lithium iron phosphate holds an almost flat voltage between about 20% and 90% charge, so voltage alone tells you little in that range.

## Label codes

| Code | Means |
|---|---|
| L... (LR6, LR03) | Alkaline, round |
| R... alone (R6, R20) | Zinc-carbon, round |
| CR... | Lithium manganese dioxide, 3 V, not rechargeable |
| BR... | Lithium carbon monofluoride, 3 V, not rechargeable |
| SR... | Silver oxide, 1.55 V |
| ICR, IMR, INR, NCR | Lithium-ion, rechargeable, 3.6–3.7 V |
| IFR, LFP | Lithium iron phosphate, rechargeable, 3.2 V |
| 18650, 21700, 14500 | Size: diameter in mm, then length in tenths of mm (18650 = 18 mm by 65 mm) |

**Look-alike warning.** 14500 lithium cells are the size of an AA, and 10440 cells the size of an AAA, but give 3.2–4.2 V, not 1.5 V. In a device made for AA or AAA cells they can destroy it or overheat. 16340 rechargeable cells look like CR123A cells but give up to 4.2 V instead of 3 V.

## Rules for every chemistry

- Match cells in a pack: same type, capacity, age and charge.
- Fuse every battery's positive lead (see skill_dc_wiring).
- Keep loose cells in cases or with taped ends.
- Swollen, leaking, dented or hot batteries are finished. See safety_swollen_lithium and safety_lead_acid.
